new_statements.quote: [p.313] As first reported by Frits Kortlandt (1975), the phonemes of Heiltsuk Wakashan include a high tone /´/ and a low tone /`/. ... Nevertheless, most instances of the Heiltsuk tones have turned out to be predictable in terms of phonotactic and morphophonemic parameters ... [p.317] (6b) The first /V/ that is both phonemically and morphophonemically a singleton, has high tone (provided rules 1, 2, and 5 are not violated), whereas following V-s satisfying the same condition, have low tone. ... [p.315] Oowekyala has accent instead of tones. In the large majority of words the accent is predictable at the phonemic level (and therefore not written by me) on the basis of the following rule, "The first /V/ of the phonemic word bears accent ..."
new_statements.citation: Rath, John C. 1985. Predictable and unpredictable tones in Heiltsuk Wakashan. Papers of the 20th International Conference on Salish and Neighbouring Languages, pp. 313-323 (quote from pp. 313, 315 and 317).
new_statements.locator: p.313 (opening paragraph); p.315 (Oowekyala accent rule); p.317 rule (6b). Verified against 300-dpi scanned files,,.
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Heiltsuk proper is a two-tone (high/low) language with tonal minimal pairs, but tone placement is largely rule-governed and culminative-like: at most three high tones per word (rule 1), a word-initial doubleton (VV) must carry a high tone (3b), and among singleton full vowels the first one takes high tone while later ones are low (6b); glottalized vowels are always low; proclitics are always low; a residue of suffix/enclitic allomorphs carries lexical (unpredictable) high tone. Rath 1974 adds that accent (stress) and length are 'linked with pitch and predictable' (accent accompanying the first high-pitched vowel for his main consultant). The Oowekyala variety has no tone but a predictable accent on the first full vowel /V/ of the phonemic word (second /V/ when the first derives from schwa). Wilson 1987 independently: Heiltsuq H tone sits where common Wakashan puts primary stress (first heavy syllable) and is synchronically phonemic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress for Heiltsuk or Oowekyala in Rath 1974/1985. Wilson 1987 p.322 states only for common Wakashan (not Heiltsuq) 'primary stress to the first heavy syllable of a word, with alternating secondary stress thereafter'.
new_statements.exceptions: Rath 1985: vocatives, interjections, borrowings, songs, onomatopoeia and full root reduplications exempt from doubleton rule 3b; singletons deriving from schwa are low unless suffix-final and word-final or before a T/R-initial enclitic (6a, 6a-1); lexical high tone in certain suffix/enclitic allomorphs (e.g. /-ba/ 'point, end', enclitic allomorph of -Rxo) and morphophonemically caused unpredictable high tones (pp.318-320). Oowekyala: when the first /V/ derives morphophonemically from schwa and is followed by [a garbled segment], 'the second /V/ of the phonemic word bears accent' (p.316). Rath 1974 3.2.2: place of accent within a pitch contour 'appears to be a matter of dialect' (speaker Freeman vs Campbell).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonemic word' = lexical word plus clitics (Rath 1985 rule 1 'lexical or combined with clitics'; proclitics always low-toned, enclitics covered by the rules). Data are elicited citation forms (Rath 1974 notes pitch 'starting-point' varies between elicited words). The Glottolog languoid heil1246 covers both Heiltsuk (tonal) and Oowekyala (non-tonal, initial-full-vowel accent); a catalog entry must say which variety it codes.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog heil1246 'Heiltsuk-Oowekyala' lumps two prosodically different varieties. Rath 1974/1985 and Wilson 1987 describe Heiltsuk proper (Bella Bella/Waglisla and Klemtu speech; Glottolog dialect bell1263 'Bella Bella' / Haíɫzaqvḷa), which is TONAL (high vs low, largely predictable, first-singleton-high). The Oowekyala variety of Rivers Inlet (Glottolog dialect oowe1239) is described in the same Rath 1985 paper (p.315-316) and in Rath 1992 fn.5 / Wilson 1987 p.321 as NON-tonal with predictable accent on the first full vowel of the phonemic word. A catalog row should code the two separately or state which one it represents.

sources.locator: p.313 (opening paragraph); p.315 (Oowekyala accent rule); p.317 rule (6b). Verified against 300-dpi scanned files,,.
sources.note: Heiltsuk: phonemic high vs low tone (Kortlandt 1975), but 'most instances of the Heiltsuk tones have turned out to be predictable'; rules 1-5 (p.314: no word has more than 3 high tones, etc.) and rule 6b (p.317: the first V that is phonemically and morphophonemically a singleton has high tone, following ones low); residue of lexical/unpredictable high tones in certain suffix/enclitic allomorphs (p.318-320). Oowekyala (p.315-316): 'has accent instead of tones', predictable: 'The first /V/ of the phonemic word bears accent' with complications when first V is in a doubleton or preceded by schwa;…

sources.note: Sec. 3.2-3.3 (printed pp.47-49): prosodic features are pitch, length and accent (stress); pitch high vs low is 'no doubt phonemic' (minimal pairs); 3.2.2 accent heard in words with a pitch contour, 'the place of the accent, however, appears to be a matter of dialect' (Freeman keeps accent with the first high-pitched vowel; Campbell differs); 3.3 'both length and accent are linked with pitch and predictable' and are not transcribed. fn.7: pitch of stem/root and suffixes interdependent, rules only partly understood.

sources.citation: Rath, John C. 1992. Notes on Boas-Hunt's North Wakashan text materials. ICSNL 27.
sources.note: fn.5: 'In the Heiltsuk transcriptions [acute] indicates high tone, in the Haisla transcriptions [acute] indicates accent. Oowekyala and Kwakwala have predictable accent which is not indicated.' Also notes 'Heiltsuk has phonemic tones' and refers to Lincoln & Rath (1980, 1986) and Rath (1981, 1985) for full range of tones/accents.

sources.citation: Wilson, Stephen A. 1987. The development of tone in Heiltsuq. Proceedings of the 13th Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society, pp. 321-329. doi:10.3765/bls.v13i0.1823
sources.note: p.323: 'Heiltsuq has two tones, high and low... A maximum of three high-toned syllables can occur in a word'; p.323-324: 'tone assignment is not predictable from synchronic segmental information, and a number of minimal pairs distinguished only by tone exist'; p.324: high tone corresponds to the common-Wakashan primary stress (first heavy syllable), never to its right; p.321: Oowekyala 'practically identical to standard Heiltsuq segmentally, but showing the common Wakashan stress system rather than tone'; p.322: common Wakashan stress = first heavy syllable, alternating secondary thereafter;…
